newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. denies Annan to see Mandela on East Timor.
newsitem.headline: U.N. denies Annan to see Mandela on East Timor.

text.p: The U.N. denied on Monday that Secretary-General Kofi Annan was to visit South Africa to brief President Nelson Mandela on the conflict in East Timor, as South Africa had announced earlier.
South African officials said Annan would arrive in Pretoria on Friday, but U.N. officials said Mandela and Annan might have misunderstood each other during an unclear cellphone conversation.
"He is definitely not going," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said, adding that he had personally spoken to Annan about the report.

He said the confusion lay in a planned visit by Annan's special representative, Jamsheed Marker, a Pakistani former U.N. ambassador, who is conducting talks at U.N. headquarters between Portuguese and Indonesian officials.
After they are completed, Marker will travel to South Africa to brief Mandela, who has offered to help the U.N. with the long-running dispute.

In a separate case of garbled communications, the Portuguese embassy in Pretoria confirmed in a statement on Monday that South Africa had expelled Portuguese Ambassador Vasco Valente last week in response to Indonesian protests about a letter that went astray.

Two South African government sources said Lisbon had been given 48 hours to withdraw Valente after it was confirmed he had received and failed to forward or return a letter from Mandela to Indonesian President Suharto, which was delivered to his embassy by mistake.

"There has been a slight mistake on the part of one individual and he has been asked to leave," said one source, adding that diplomatic relations with Portugal remained intact. Valente was the first foreign diplomat expelled since 1994, when Mandela won the country's first democratic elections.

In the letter, Mandela asked Suharto to release jailed rebel leader Xanana Gusmao as a first step towards ending the conflict in East Timor, a former Portuguese colony of which Indonesia has taken control.
Details of the letter were published in Portuguese newspapers before Suharto knew of its existence, undermining Mandela's effort to assist the U.N. peace initiative.

East Timor is the third international conflict in which Mandela has sought personally to intervene. He has tried to help bring democracy to Nigeria and sought to mediate a peaceful transfer of power in the former Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Mandela visited Suharto last month and won permission to meet the jailed rebel leader Gusmao. He also invited East Timorese bishop and Nobel peace laureate Ximenes Belo to visit him in South Africa.

Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 after a civil war erupted following Portugal's withdrawal from its colony. In 1976 Indonesia incorporated the territory as its 27th province but this has never been recognised by the United Nations.
